reviews.title: Text Limits Make It Unusable
reviews.text:
The new text limits make copilot unusable. Microsoft seems to have little to no respect for their customers. 

This is a recurring theme with Microsoft where every product or service seems like you’re trapped or forced into something. You integrate copilot into your routines, set preferences, learn the nuances etc. then later the terms change and you’re forced to either uproot your routine or pay them to keep using what you structured everything around.  

High text limits I could understand, or image limits or advanced thinking limits, a few thousand texts to limit abuse maybe in the quick think mode, but these limits are as little as 2-3 messages, making the free tier completely useless.

They also tried to trap or force people into using bing with copilot before, making it a tiny window in the bing app as if bing is this super app and copilot is just an accessory you sometimes use. 

Why can’t Microsoft just make products people want to use and then offer paid options people will want to pay for? You know, like practically every other company. Why’s everything have to be some little scheme or trick or marketing ploy to force or coerce or trap people into using or paying for their products?

I won’t be using copilot anymore until there’s no text limits, and even then only if the multiple other competing AI’s start trying to do the same.

Next, they’ve put this nag bubble on the iPhone version that says get more done with copilot and an upgrade button. There’s no way to dismiss the message, and it comes over the top of other things on your screen, so there’s no way to see what’s underneath.

They really should have held off on disabling the “legacy” copilot app functionality until the full functionality was in the new iOS app.

reviews.title: 👎👎 Stop suspending accounts for testing image prompts
reviews.text:
Account warnings for failed generations are ridiculous. Don’t punish users for experimenting with image ideas. Suspension threats for simple prompt testing must go. Let people test the AI without risking their account. 

Stop suspending accounts for testing image prompts. This feature is poorly designed and actively harms your product. Showing (or enforcing) account suspension warnings simply because a user experiments with different image generation ideas is wrong. If the model or app cannot handle one or two prompts, the correct response is a clear “unable to generate” message — not a threat to the user’s account. 

Punishing exploration stops people from testing the actual limits and capabilities of the AI. Users should be free to try varied ideas without fear of warnings or suspensions; that is how people discover what works, what doesn’t, and where the tool can improve. Turning failed generations into account-level risks is counterproductive, discourages legitimate creative use, and makes the app feel unreliable and hostile to its own users. 

Please remove the suspension warnings (and any actual suspensions) that are triggered merely by attempting prompts the system cannot fulfil. Let people experiment freely. A simple refusal is enough; threatening the account is not.

reviews.title: Former Favorite AI, Now a Huge Disappointment
reviews.text:
This used to be my favorite AI app. The Projects feature was what made Copilot different from every other chatbot. I used it to save important information, track ongoing topics, and build on previous conversations over time.

Then the update arrived and Projects were just gone.

The most frustrating part is that there was little to no warning. Users weren't given a chance to download, export, or save the information they had spent months creating before it disappeared. Losing that data feels like a slap in the face to loyal users.

Now there are chat limits, constant prompts to upgrade, and very little transparency about what the paid version actually includes or costs. After seeing major features removed without warning, why should users trust that an upgrade won't lead to more surprises down the road?

What made Copilot special was stripped away. The free version now feels like a basic chatbot experience that I can get from countless other apps or even a Google search without the same restrictions.

It honestly feels like users were encouraged to invest time and information into the platform, only to have key features removed and replaced with limitations. Instead of making me want to upgrade, this update has made me look at other AI options.

A real shame. Copilot went from being my go-to AI assistant to something I barely recognize or use.

reviews.title: The only use for this AI was to save time on writing this one star review
reviews.text:
I rarely leave one‑star reviews, but this app absolutely deserves it.
I used Copilot to create a presentation from a PDF. The iPad app failed to do this, so I switched to my PC and used Copilot inside PowerPoint. That part worked. I saved the presentation to OneDrive as instructed.
From there, everything fell apart.
On the iPad, Copilot shows all my chat titles, but when I tap them I get a useless message: “You can’t open this chat.” No explanation. No guidance. No workaround. Just a dead end.
This is not an intelligence problem — it’s a product design failure:
• Chats appear synced but are not usable
• File‑based Copilot conversations are locked to desktop without warning
• The app knows the chats exist but cannot explain why they are blocked
• Mobile is clearly a second‑class citizen
If a chat is tied to PowerPoint, a PDF, or desktop‑only capabilities, the app should say so clearly instead of pretending something is wrong with the user.
The irony is painful: a competing AI produced a full PowerPoint presentation from the same PDF in seconds, while Copilot required multiple apps, devices, and still failed to deliver a usable cross‑platform workflow.

reviews.title: 🪄 The Magic Trick No One Asked For 🪄
reviews.text:

365 Copilot Chat spent months stumbling around like it had just woken up from a coma — until one miraculous update transformed it into a genuinely brilliant tool. It was sharp, capable, even enjoyable. For a brief moment, it seemed like Microsoft had finally found that sweet spot.

Naturally, that meant it had to be removed immediately.

In its place: Office Agent, the kind of magician who walks onstage, drops the deck of cards, forgets the rabbit, and then pulls a wilted handkerchief out of an empty hat as if that was the trick all along.

If you’re considering paying for a subscription, make sure the trial is long enough to witness the magic trick before your money disappears along with the features.
